summary: Guderian’s forces try to bypass Tula toward Venev, Kashira and the Oka approaches. Soviet resistance and exposed communications prevent movement from becoming a secure encirclement.
body:
A city that still blocked the road

Tula remained an obstacle because its defenders continued to function. German forces could move around the city, threaten its communications, and reach settlements farther east without extinguishing the Soviet army and industrial community inside it. On 18 November 1941, Heinz Guderian renewed the southern offensive toward Moscow under precisely those conditions. His Second Panzer Army was expected to turn movement beyond Tula into the southern arm of a much larger envelopment. It would have to do so while containing a defended city behind its leading formations and protecting an increasingly exposed eastern flank.[1]

The opening produced a striking local advance. The U.S. Army history reports that one of Guderian's corps covered almost twenty-five miles during the first day. Read alone, that distance suggests the return of the mobile warfare that had carried German forces across enormous stretches of the Soviet Union. Read beside the condition of the army and the tasks still ahead, it becomes more ambiguous. A fast spearhead could reach a new objective before the infantry needed to secure the route, while the surviving Soviet positions continued to threaten the forces passing them. Tactical momentum and operational vulnerability grew together.[1]

The opening study of this phase traced the decision to renew the offensive. At Tula, its risks became immediate. Guderian needed roads through Stalinogorsk and Venev to carry his forces toward Kashira, while the Fiftieth Army still held the city on his western side. Moscow remained a distant objective beyond that unfinished battle. Every formation sent north had to be supplied through country the Germans had only just entered, and every detachment left behind to protect it reduced the force available at the front. Tula's survival would give the Soviet command time and positions from which to contest the bypass.[1]

The defence behind the name

The Fiftieth Army had survived the destruction of the Bryansk position in October in a badly damaged condition. Its defence of Tula drew on regular formations and local resources, including the Tula Workers' Regiment, the 156th NKVD Rifle Regiment, and the 108th Tank Division. These components were not interchangeable. Infantry, tanks, artillery, security troops, and workers organized for combat contributed different capabilities. Holding the city required them to function as parts of a defence rather than as a collection of heroic names. A surviving headquarters and a working system for issuing orders were as important as the determination to stand.[2][1]

On 10 November, the Fiftieth Army had come under Zhukov's Western Front. This brought Tula into the same front command responsible for the principal Moscow approaches and made the southern defence part of a broader allocation of forces. Command responsibility mattered because the danger did not stop at a city boundary. An enemy move east of Tula could threaten roads connecting neighbouring armies, while a Soviet counterattack near the Oka could prevent German forces farther west from helping Guderian. The local battle and the wider front therefore influenced one another even when their soldiers could not see the same battlefield.[1]

Tula's industrial role made this relationship unusually tangible. Evacuation had removed much of its productive capacity, yet remaining facilities continued to manufacture weapons and repair equipment. A factory could be part of national evacuation policy and still leave behind workers and machinery performing urgent local tasks. The distinction helps explain how a threatened industrial city could support its own defence while losing much of the economic activity that had defined it before the war. Production continued under military necessity and severe disruption, rather than under anything resembling ordinary factory conditions.[2]

A workers' regiment begins with a decision

The surviving catalogue of Tula's wartime documents identifies a city defence committee resolution of 23 October establishing the Workers' Regiment. It locates the original in the former regional party archive and records its publication in the collection Battle for Tula. The catalogue establishes the decision and its date; it does not by itself establish every man's motive, training, or conduct in battle. The document's existence nevertheless restores an institutional step often lost in commemorative accounts. Workers had to be organized into a formation before their participation could become a military capability.[3]

Evacuation and local defence placed competing demands on Tula's workforce. Sending machinery east preserved future production; keeping skilled workers and usable equipment in the city supported the soldiers defending it now. The workers' regiment added another demand for men who might otherwise have remained in a workshop. Tula's industrial contribution consequently included both the plant that left and the repairs or manufacture that continued. Its inhabitants were caught inside these decisions, maintaining an endangered city while parts of the community departed. The defence drew strength from that work, but it also consumed the labour and resources on which civilian life depended.[3][2]

The bypass opens

Guderian's postwar account describes an army spreading across several routes. The Eighteenth Panzer Division advanced toward Yefremov, where he records street fighting on 20 November. The Tenth Motorized Division moved through Yepifan toward Mikhaylov; the Twenty-Ninth Motorized Division covered the eastern side around Spasskoye and Gremyacheye. Farther north, the Seventeenth Panzer Division would be directed toward Kashira. These assignments placed formations at different distances from Tula and gave them different responsibilities. Guderian later presented the exposed flank as a central explanation of his failure, but his own itinerary also shows how widely his orders distributed the army's remaining strength.[4]

The names on that itinerary describe different problems. Stalinogorsk lay in the industrial country east of Tula; Venev offered a route farther north; Kashira stood on the Oka system and mattered for movement toward the capital's southern approaches. Reaching one place did not secure the others. Nor could a force directed toward an Oka crossing assume that the surrounding roads and rear areas were safe. A column's position on a map might look like the beginning of an encirclement while the space behind it still contained organized Soviet troops capable of fighting, withdrawing, or striking its communications.[1][4]

The first day's movement is therefore best understood as an opening. It exposed parts of the Soviet defence and created opportunities for further German advances. It did not produce a completed ring around Tula, still less a connection with the German northern armies. Those larger results required additional fighting and coordination. The offensive's apparent speed was also uneven: mobile troops could exploit a local breach while exhausted infantry and supply columns followed more slowly. The farther those elements separated, the more the army depended on being able to improvise protection with forces needed somewhere else.[1][5]

Fresh Soviet troops complicated the advance almost immediately. The 239th Rifle Division entered the fighting around Stalinogorsk and contested the area through which German formations were attempting to move north. Its presence forced the attackers to fight for their route and then attempt another encirclement before they could turn fully toward their larger objectives. Guderian's account acknowledges the division's resistance and its later escape. The episode is especially revealing because his explanation was intended to describe German operational problems: even there, Soviet troops appear as an active opponent disrupting the sequence of the advance, rather than a force simply waiting for the winter to intervene.[2][4]

Guderian also recorded a disturbing incident immediately before the renewed offensive. On 17 November, the 112th Infantry Division encountered fresh Soviet opposition near Uzlovaya and tanks coming from Dedilovo. His account describes panic spreading back toward Bogoroditsk before the neighbouring 167th Infantry Division helped restore the situation. The description is retrospective and comes from the army commander, but it is an unusually explicit admission that German infantry could lose cohesion under pressure. It also gives Soviet action its proper place in the story: German exhaustion became a battlefield disadvantage because an opponent was present to exploit it.[4]

The assignments Guderian listed for 18 November show how much of his force was already occupied with supporting tasks. The Eighteenth Panzer Division was directed toward Yefremov, the Tenth Motorized Division toward Yepifan and Mikhaylov, and the Twenty-Ninth Motorized Division toward the eastern flank. These movements supported the larger operation but did not all point directly toward Moscow. A tally of the army's divisions therefore exaggerates the strength available for any single thrust if it assumes that every formation could be concentrated against the same objective. The army had to move through and hold a broad area while still finding force for its principal operation.[4]

The subsequent escape of the 239th Rifle Division had a similarly concrete cost on both sides. Guderian acknowledged that Soviet troops broke through the thin line of the Twenty-Ninth Motorized Division, leaving equipment and artillery behind while saving personnel. The loss of those weapons mattered for the division's future combat effectiveness; surviving men did not immediately constitute a fully equipped replacement formation. For the Germans, however, a pocket that required containment and then failed to destroy its occupants was an expensive result. It demanded combat strength without securing the removal of all the enemy personnel that the operation had intended to eliminate.[4]

The German command tried to repair these weaknesses by finding more infantry. Guderian records that the 112th Division needed relief and that the Fifty-Sixth Infantry Division was to be brought forward from the Karachev area. This was a transfer between existing commitments, with a journey still to be completed. The relief could not protect every new stretch of the salient at once. Soviet resistance around Stalinogorsk had thus created demands extending beyond the immediate battlefield: a fresh German formation had to move, take over responsibilities, and release troops whose original mission had already been disrupted.[4]

The projected strike against Soviet communications provides another measure of the operation’s limits. Guderian’s retrospective account records the importance attached to cutting the Ryazan–Kolomna railway, which supported the Soviet position beyond his eastern flank. After reaching Mikhaylov on 27 November, the Tenth Motorized Division sent reconnaissance and demolition parties toward that railway, but they did not reach the intended target. This later development clarifies the ambition behind the movement that began on 18 November. Taking an intermediate town and dispatching a patrol were steps toward disrupting Soviet reinforcement; they were not proof that the railway had been severed. The distinction preserves the difference between an operational order, a reconnaissance effort, and an achieved interdiction.[4]

A flank is an obligation

The central difficulty was the shape of Guderian's advance. His leading troops were being directed northward, but Soviet forces could approach their eastern side from the Ryazan and Kolomna directions. Second Army, farther south, could not simply provide an unbroken protective wall, while Fourth Army had its own difficulties around the Oka. The farther the Second Panzer Army advanced, the longer the vulnerable side of its operation became. Protecting it required troops, reconnaissance, and reserves that were also needed for the main attack. Guderian's later emphasis on this problem was self-interested, but the geography and the continuing Soviet activity made it real.[4][1]

West of Tula, Guderian's Forty-Third Army Corps faced a different task from the mobile troops racing east. Its Thirty-First and 131st Infantry Divisions operated between the Upa and Oka, with Aleksin among the relevant approaches. Their advance was supposed to help reduce Tula and connect the operation toward Fourth Army. Meanwhile, formations on the opposite side of the city had to cover approaches from Ryazan and Kolomna. The army was trying to compress one flank around a defended city while extending the other into open country. The infantry needed for the first task could not simply be transferred to the second without weakening the attempted encirclement.[4]

The Soviet counterblows near Serpukhov made the German dilemma worse. Kluge's Fourth Army had to fight for its own position when Bock wanted it to help complete the larger operation. Some of its regiments were so depleted that their remaining men and junior officers could not reasonably be treated as fresh attacking formations. This was not merely a quarrel among generals about enthusiasm. A neighbouring army that could not move across its own obstacle could not close the gap on another commander's schedule. The southern pincer consequently depended on events that Guderian could influence only indirectly.[1]

German success had often depended on accepting flank risks in order to dislocate an opponent before he could respond. In November, however, Soviet resistance was surviving long enough for the consequences of that risk to accumulate. The Fiftieth Army remained at Tula, the Oka remained a significant barrier, and fresh Soviet forces were being directed toward the endangered approaches. Continued advance could therefore enlarge an army's commitments without correspondingly reducing the enemy's capacity to interfere. The operational method depended increasingly on an enemy collapse that had yet to occur.[1]

Shelter as a military resource

The harshness of the southern battle reached into civilian homes. On 17 November, the Stavka issued Order No. 0428 directing the destruction of settlements behind German lines to deprive the invaders of shelter. It authorized aircraft, artillery, and small raiding parties, and instructed Soviet forces withdrawing from an area to take the population with them while destroying places the enemy could use. The order's premise was that accommodation had become a resource on which German endurance depended. Its human implications were equally clear: houses and villages could be sacrificed in the pursuit of military advantage.[6]

The order prescribed destruction in a belt forty to sixty kilometres behind the German front and twenty to thirty kilometres to either side of roads. It directed the formation of raiding parties of twenty to thirty men. Those distances describe the command's intended reach, rather than a verified record of every settlement destroyed. They reveal the scale of a policy that treated civilian shelter as part of the enemy's supply arrangements. The accompanying requirement to remove inhabitants offered no assurance of sufficient transport, food or alternative accommodation. Military denial could leave a family without a home even when Soviet forces later recovered its village.[6]

German requisition and occupation placed their own demands on these communities. The Stavka order itself described villagers being driven from shelter by German troops; that assertion should be recognized as the issuing command's account, rather than treated as a complete survey. More broadly, the competition for shelter reveals how inadequate it is to discuss winter only as an encounter between soldiers and temperature. Warmth depended on buildings, fuel, clothing, food, and the power to obtain them. Armies exercised that power over people whose own survival depended on the same things.[6][5]

Guderian's own later description of his infantry makes the importance of shelter and rest more concrete. He portrayed an army of twelve exhausted divisions whose marching infantry could sometimes manage only five to ten kilometres in a day. This was his retrospective assessment, not a measured speed for every formation. It is nevertheless a striking contrast with the nearly twenty-five miles attributed to a leading corps on 18 November. An armoured column's opening dash and the daily capacity of the men following it belonged to different stages of the same operation. The widening interval between them exposed the roads that kept the advance supplied.[4][1]

Toward Kashira and the counterstroke

The advance beyond 18 November developed through several further engagements. German forces pushed through the country east of Tula and toward the approaches to Kashira, while Soviet commanders attempted to contain the penetration. It is important to keep these subsequent events in sequence. The threat to Kashira belongs to the later November fighting; it was not a completed achievement of the opening day. The Seventeenth Panzer Division's northward movement helped form the large bulge around Tula described in the official history, but the city continued to resist inside the threatened arc.[1]

Pavel Belov's cavalry corps helped oppose the later threat to Kashira, alongside tank and infantry forces. On 26 November his Second Cavalry Corps became the First Guards Cavalry Corps, a redesignation publicly announced in Pravda the following day. The award recognized an existing formation, not the sudden assembly of a new corps. Cavalry gave Soviet commanders a means of moving armed men where motor transport was scarce, but successful action still depended on support, ammunition and coordination. Belov's troops contested the approaches on which Guderian's northern movement depended. Their intervention threatened a spearhead already connected to its rear by an increasingly vulnerable stretch of road.[7][1]

An army still arriving

The Tenth Army would eventually strengthen the region beyond Guderian's eastern flank, but its movement belonged to the last week of November. Its commander, Filipp Golikov, received marching orders on 24 November. The army had to cover the long journey from Syzran by rail and on foot because it possessed little motor transport. Its appearance on a strategic map therefore represented a process unfolding over days. A headquarters assignment could precede the arrival of all the troops needed to carry it out.[1]

This sequence explains why German commanders could experience Soviet strength as a succession of unwelcome surprises. The reinforcements did not have to arrive everywhere at once to frustrate an offensive. A new force at a threatened crossing could prevent an immediate success; another formation farther east could make an exposed flank harder to ignore. German troops then spent additional time and ammunition solving problems outside their original objective. Soviet reinforcement was uneven and costly, but its cumulative effect was to deprive the attacker of the uninterrupted sequence on which his larger design depended.[1]

What the southern advance meant

The southern pincer demonstrates why kilometres alone provide an inadequate measure of an offensive. A formation could travel quickly on one day and still finish the week less able to complete its mission. It might gain ground while leaving a defended city behind, expend fuel without gaining a usable railway, or create a salient that demanded more troops than it released. Guderian's force remained dangerous, and Soviet commanders could not dismiss its progress. Yet the relationship between movement and strategic effect was becoming less favourable to the Germans with each new obligation.[1]

The wider war was also moving on 18 November. Britain opened Operation Crusader in North Africa, adding pressure in another theatre while Anglo-American assistance to the Soviet Union developed. That operation was not an immediate rescue for a particular Soviet battalion near Tula, and it should not be inserted into the local battle as though it were. It did, however, underline the German strategic problem: the eastern campaign was continuing while other commitments remained active. German planning could no longer assume that defeating the Soviet Union would quickly release its resources for a different war.[8][5]

Tula's defenders had made that wider failure concrete. By holding the city, sustaining military organization, and preserving useful local capacities, they forced the attackers to keep spending resources on a problem that the plan required them to leave behind. Their achievement was neither effortless nor inevitable. It included dangerous penetrations, encircled Soviet formations, strained communications, and civilians whose lives were subordinated to the demands of survival and defence. The city remained a functioning obstacle because people continued to make it one.[2][1]

Later attempts to close the ring would continue into December and belong to the study of the advance's limits. Meanwhile, farther south, German forces were approaching a different city whose capture appeared to promise a major strategic gain. The fall of Rostov would test another version of the same question: whether the army taking an important place could also secure the conditions necessary to hold it.[1]
